subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 10 periods = 400 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

periods.activity_title: First Encounter: Reading the Poem Aloud

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the poem “The Rainbow” aloud at a measured pace, with rising emphasis at each ‘But’ and a contemplative tone at the final lines. Students listen with books open at pp.27–28.
Teacher models a second read-aloud, pausing after each stanza to invite students to notice one image or sound they liked. Students share one observation each in a quick round.
Whole-class choral reading of both stanzas twice: first quietly, then with growing confidence. Teacher coaches the group to lift their voices at ‘prettier far’ each time it appears.
Teacher draws attention to the two stanzas’ parallel structure — boats and ships in the first, bridges in the second — and asks students to name what each stanza compares before the sitting closes.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem’s power rests on its cumulative comparison: each ‘But’ raises the stakes before the final revelation of the rainbow. Watch that students do not rush the word ‘overtops’ — it is the poem’s most unusual verb and worth a brief pause to savour its meaning.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think A (p.28): discuss meaning of ‘bow’, preferred bridge, pronoun ‘these’, and four True/False statements.

time_bands.activity: Students re-read the poem silently at p.27–28 while teacher writes the four True/False statements on the board for reference during discussion.

Let us Think A (p.28) — teacher leads oral discussion of questions 1, 2 and 3: the meaning of ‘bow’ as an arch, which bridge the poet prefers and why, and what ‘these’ refers to in each stanza. Students give answers in full sentences.

Let us Think A (p.28) — students work in pairs on the four True/False items (ships/rivers, boats/seas, bridges/rivers, road/earth to sky). Pairs then share verdicts and justify each using a line from the poem.
Class debriefs the True/False verdicts together. Teacher highlights how the poem deliberately inverts expectations (boats on rivers, not seas) and asks students what effect this contrast creates.

periods.teacher_notes: A common slip is reading ‘bow’ only as the weapon; guide students to notice Rossetti’s use of it to mean both an arch and the rainbow’s curved shape. The pronoun ‘these’ shifts its reference between stanzas — point students to the specific nouns in each stanza rather than expecting intuitive recall.

periods.activity_title: Discussion and Listening: Rhyming Words Circle

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think B (p.28): guided discussion on crossing rivers, personal rainbow memory, and imagining walking a rainbow.
Let us Listen (p.30): teacher reads each word aloud; students respond with five rhyming words in a circle.

time_bands.activity: Let us Think B (p.28) — teacher poses the three discussion prompts in turn: ways to cross a river, personal memories of seeing a rainbow, and the imaginative question of where a rainbow road might lead. Students respond in full sentences, building on each other’s ideas.

Teacher asks the class to arrange their chairs in a circle and explains the listening task: she will read a word aloud and each student contributes one rhyming word in turn, going round the circle until five rhymes are collected.

Let us Listen (p.30) — teacher reads each of the ten words (ship, tree, bow, rain, sun, sea, sail, and, sky, far) aloud clearly, one at a time, with a brief pause between. Students respond round the circle; teacher accepts any phonetically valid rhyme and notes varied responses on the board.
Brief whole-class reflection: which word generated the most varied rhymes? Teacher draws attention to words from the poem (bow, sea, far) and notes how rhyme-sound connects to the poem’s own music.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening task prioritises sound over spelling — accept all phonetically valid rhymes for each word. For the discussion prompts, watch that the imaginative question about walking a rainbow does not get cut short; it often generates the richest language and is worth an unhurried pause.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak (p.30): recite the two companion poems in happy, angry and surprised voices.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads ‘Colours’ (p.30) aloud in a happy voice, then ‘Aachoo!’ (p.30) in a surprised voice as demonstrations. Students listen and identify which vocal qualities — pitch, pace, stress — signal each emotion.

Let us Speak (p.30) — class is divided into three groups. Each group rehearses one of the three voices (happy, angry, surprised) for ‘Colours.’ Groups then perform in turn while the others listen and guess the emotion from vocal cues alone.

Let us Speak (p.30) — the same three-voice exercise with ‘Aachoo!’ Each group performs; teacher coaches particular attention to the elephant’s sneeze line and the sales girl’s surprised response as natural dramatic moments.

Whole-class reflection: students name one word or line in either poem that felt easiest to make expressive. Teacher connects this observation to the idea that word choice shapes how a poem feels when spoken aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: The ‘angry voice’ tends to flatten into shouting; remind students that an angry voice can also be low and controlled. The dialogue in ‘Aachoo!’ between the elephant and the sales girl is a natural prompt for role-play if energy allows.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn A (p.29): rearrange scrambled letters to form words from the poem.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the first scrambled word ‘sial’ on the board and works through the unscrambling process aloud, locating ‘sail’ in the poem’s first line (p.27). Students see the connection between the activity and the poem’s own vocabulary.

Let us Learn A (p.29) — students work individually to unscramble the remaining eight words (vierr, sae, oduscl, risebgd, nhveea, eoptvros, owb, droa). Teacher circulates, prompting students to check their answer by finding the word in the poem.

Pairs swap their answers and verify each unscrambled word against the poem text. Teacher calls on different pairs to share each answer, building the complete set on the board and briefly noting where in the poem each word appears.

Quick spoken round: teacher points to any five of the nine words on the board at random and individual students read them aloud confidently. Teacher notes any word that causes hesitation for further attention.

periods.teacher_notes: The word ‘eoptvros’ (overtops) is the longest and most unfamiliar; give it extra time and ask students what they think it means before they look it up in the poem. Connecting each unscrambled word to its line in the poem reinforces reading fluency alongside the word-building work.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn B (p.29): paired spinning-circle poetry exploration game — title, rhymes, images, instrument, repeated words.
Let us Write D (p.36): write opposites beginning with ‘S’ for ten given words.

time_bands.activity: Let us Learn B (p.29) — students work in pairs with the spinning-circle. One partner moves a finger; when stopped, both respond to that segment’s prompt (new title, rhyming pairs, mental images, musical instrument, repeated words). Pairs work through at least three segments each.
Brief share-out: teacher collects one response per segment from different pairs, recording the rhyming pairs and repeated words on the board to confirm accuracy against the poem.

Let us Write D (p.36) — teacher models the first answer (large × small) and explains the constraint that every opposite must begin with ‘S.’ Students work individually to complete items b through k (strong, slow, smooth, shiny/sparkling, straight, stop, subtraction, simple, sharp/spicy).
Quick whole-class check: teacher reads out each clue word and students call out their ‘S’ answer. Teacher acknowledges all valid responses, since some clues admit more than one correct answer.

periods.teacher_notes: Several clues in the S-opposites activity have more than one defensible answer (e.g. ‘dull’ could yield ‘sharp’ or ‘shiny’ or ‘sparkling’); accept any that begin with S and are semantically valid rather than insisting on a single answer. The spinning-circle game works best if pairs are given a moment to look at the poem before starting, so the poem text is accessible on the desk.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write F (p.37): identify colours and mother-tongue names for nine kitchen spices.

homework.task_brief: Let us Write D (p.36): make sentences in notebook using the ten S-opposite words written in class.

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a quick connection to the rainbow’s spectrum of colours studied in the poem and asks students to name as many colours as they can. This bridges the poem’s imagery to the colour-observation task ahead.

Let us Write F (p.37) — teacher displays or names the nine kitchen items (clove, cinnamon, dry chilli, garlic, curry leaves, peppercorns, fennel seeds, cumin seeds, mustard seeds) and models the first entry. Students complete the two-column table (colour and mother-tongue name) in their notebooks, drawing on personal observation and discussion with a partner.

Students share their colour descriptions and mother-tongue names aloud in a brief round. Teacher notes where students’ observations differ (e.g. garlic described as white, cream or pale yellow) and celebrates the linguistic diversity of names.
Teacher sets homework: use the ten S-opposite words written in the previous sitting to make sentences in their notebooks, following the model from Let us Write D (p.36).

periods.teacher_notes: This task intentionally links colour observation to lived experience and home language, so varied answers are a strength rather than a problem. Students who are uncertain of a colour should be encouraged to describe it in their own words rather than leave the column blank.
materials: If available: sample spices or pictures of each for observation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write B (p.34): complete the compound-word table using word-joining patterns including rainbow, teacup, wristwatch.
Let us Write C (p.35): write two sentences per word — once as noun, once as verb — for five selected words.

time_bands.activity: Let us Write B (p.34) — teacher opens with the example ‘rain + bow = rainbow’ from the poem and explains how two smaller words join to make one new word. Students complete the nine-row compound-word table individually, using the picture clues on p.34 as guides.

Pairs check their compound-word answers against each other and resolve any differences by looking at the picture clues. Teacher confirms the full set with the class and writes any unfamiliar compounds (earring, wristwatch) on the board.

Let us Write C (p.35) — teacher models the noun-verb distinction with the worked example ‘bridge’ from p.35, then asks students to choose five words from the ten given (cut, bat, picture, cry, filter, dance, plant, paint, fly, face) and write two sentences for each — one as a noun and one as a verb — in their notebooks.
Two or three students read one of their noun-verb sentence pairs aloud. The class identifies which sentence uses the word as a noun and which as a verb, explaining their reasoning briefly.

periods.teacher_notes: The compound-word table includes items (earring, wristwatch, armchair) where students must supply both component words; direct them to look at the picture clue carefully before writing. For the noun-verb task, ‘picture’ and ‘plant’ often trip students — the worked example on p.35 is worth re-reading together before they begin.

periods.activity_title: Travel Paragraph: Plan, Draft and Share

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write A (p.34): plan and draft an 80–100-word paragraph about a personal travel experience.

time_bands.activity: Teacher re-reads the first stanza of ‘The Rainbow’ (p.27) to recall the poem’s imagery of boats and ships travelling across water, then connects this to the writing task: students will write about a journey of their own.

Guided planning: teacher writes the six prompt categories from Let us Write A (p.34) on the board — destination and time, purpose, companions, likes and dislikes, local food, landmark/scenery — and students spend this time jotting brief notes against each, choosing one real or imagined journey.

Let us Write A (p.34) — students draft their 80–100-word paragraph in their notebooks, using their planning notes. Teacher circulates, offering brief formative prompts on sentence connection and vocabulary rather than correcting line by line.

Three or four students read their completed paragraph aloud. After each reading, teacher invites one peer observation about a vivid detail or well-chosen word, then closes the sitting with brief encouragement about the class’s range of destinations and voices.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who have not travelled far may write about an imagined or very local journey — a walk to the market, a visit to a grandparent — so the task remains inclusive. Encourage specific sensory detail over general statements; the six planning prompts are designed to draw out concrete observations.

periods.activity_title: Colour Mixing, Flowerpot Friend and Boats Exploration

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do (p.39): colour the six mixing diagrams and write the resulting colour name for each combination.
Let us Explore B (p.40): group discussion — human-made things versus natural things; share observations with the class.

homework.task_brief: Let us Write G (p.38): design and colour a Flowerpot Friend in the blank outline provided.

time_bands.activity: Let us Do (p.39) — students colour the six mixing diagrams individually and complete the partially-spelled colour names (purple, green, orange, pink, maroon, brown). Teacher connects the activity to the rainbow’s spectrum, noting that mixing primary colours produces the secondary colours visible in a rainbow.

Teacher shares the Did You Know fact about Isaac Newton’s spinning disc (p.40) orally — that white light contains all colours, revealed when the disc slows. Students briefly discuss in pairs what this tells them about sunlight and the rainbow.

Let us Explore B (p.40) — class is split into two groups: one discusses human-made things from the poem (ships, bridges) and the other discusses natural things (clouds, rainbows). Each group appoints a speaker to share three observations with the full class.

Teacher sets homework: complete the Flowerpot Friend design in the blank outline on p.38, adding colour and any accessories the student chooses. Teacher briefly shows the three completed examples as reference before students leave.

periods.teacher_notes: The colour-mixing task is directly linked to the rainbow’s colours discussed throughout the chapter — encourage students to notice that purple, green, and orange all appear in a rainbow’s arc. The group discussion in Let us Explore B works best when groups are given a moment to list their points quietly before the share-out begins.

items.source_lo: Student interprets meaning and comparative structure in a poem using a two-stanza poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Rossetti’s rainbow poem: meaning of ‘bow’, pronoun ‘these’, True/False statements about boats, ships, bridges.
items.item_stem: In the poem ‘The Rainbow,’ Christina Rossetti uses the word ‘bow’ to describe the rainbow. Which of the following best explains why she chose that word?

options.label: A
options.text: The rainbow curves across the sky the way an arch or bow curves.

options.label: B
options.text: The rainbow is used as a weapon, like an archer’s bow.

options.label: C
options.text: The rainbow looks like the bow tied on a gift.

options.label: D
options.text: The rainbow makes a bowing motion like a person greeting someone.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Suggests the student is thinking of the word’s most familiar meaning without applying it to the poem’s imagery.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Reveals a literal reading that treats ‘bow’ as an action rather than a shape.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Shows the student is associating ‘bow’ with a different everyday object rather than the poem’s structural metaphor.

items.source_lo: Student interprets meaning and comparative structure in a poem using a two-stanza poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Rossetti’s rainbow poem: meaning of ‘bow’, pronoun ‘these’, True/False statements about boats, ships, bridges.
items.item_stem: In the poem, the word ‘these’ appears at the end of both stanzas in the phrase ‘prettier far than these.’ Read the page 27 poem carefully and explain: what does ‘these’ refer to in the first stanza, and what does it refer to in the second stanza? Write two sentences.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: In the first stanza, ‘these’ refers to the boats on the rivers and the ships on the seas. In the second stanza, ‘these’ refers to the man-made bridges on the rivers.

items.source_lo: Student listens attentively and generates rhyming words orally using a circle listening activity as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Rhyming-word circle using ten words from the poem (ship, tree, bow, rain, sun, sea, sail, and, sky, far).
items.item_stem: Your teacher will read the word ‘sky’ aloud twice. Listen carefully and then say two words that rhyme with ‘sky.’

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Statements 1 and 3 are true: ‘high’ and ‘fly’ rhyme with ‘sky.’ Statements 2 and 4 are false: ‘see’ ends in the ‘ee’ sound and ‘sail’ ends in the ‘ail’ sound, neither matching the ‘-y/i’ sound of ‘sky.’

items.item_stem: Say aloud three words that rhyme with ‘rain.’ Your teacher will listen for sound, not spelling — any word that sounds like ‘rain’ at the end will count.

expected_elements: Three words ending in the ‘-ain/-ane/-eign’ sound.
Each word pronounced clearly and distinctly.
Any phonetically valid rhyme accepted (train, plain, cane, main).

items.source_lo: Student recites a poem expressively with voice modulation using short poems as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Recitation of ‘Colours’ and ‘Aachoo!’ in happy, angry and surprised voices.
items.item_stem: Listen to the line from ‘Aachoo!’ on page 30 beginning ‘A hanky for an elephant?’ — is the sales girl’s voice here meant to sound happy, surprised, or angry? Choose the correct answer.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Suggests the student has not read the situation: a sales girl faced with an impossible request would not naturally sound happy.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Reveals a misreading of the tone; the poem’s humour depends on the sales girl’s astonishment, not annoyance.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Shows the student may be confusing emotional tone with a general negative reaction rather than reading the comedic context.

expected_elements: Voice is bright, lively and upbeat in tone.
Lines spoken clearly with correct word order.
Emphasis placed on the idea of sharing crayons.

items.item_stem: The poem ‘The Rainbow’ imagines the rainbow as a road that goes from earth to sky. Think of a journey you have taken or would like to take. Write three sentences describing where you went (or would go), who was with you, and one thing you noticed or enjoyed on the way.

expected_elements: Names a destination or direction of travel.
Mentions at least one companion or states travelling alone.
Includes a specific observation or liked detail.

items.item_stem: Fill in the new colour that each mixing combination produces.
items.visual_stimulus:
Colours mixed | New colour
red + blue | _______
yellow + blue | _______
red + yellow | _______
red + white | _______

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: red + blue → purple; yellow + blue → green; red + yellow → orange; red + white → pink.

items.item_stem: In the poem, Rossetti compares human-made things (like bridges and ships) with natural things (like clouds and the rainbow). Choose one human-made thing and one natural thing from the poem and tell your teacher: what can the human-made thing do that the natural one cannot, and what can the natural thing do that the human-made one cannot?

expected_elements: Names one human-made and one natural thing from the poem.
States a capability unique to the human-made thing.
States a capability or quality unique to the natural thing.
